content.text:
Operator
Good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to the Cross Country Healthcare's Earnings Conference Call for the Q3 2022. Please be advised that this call is being recorded, and a replay of this webcast will be available on the company's website. Details for accessing the audio replay can be found on the company's earnings re-issued this afternoon. At the conclusion of the prepared remarks, I will open the lines for questions. I would now like to turn the call over to Josh Vogel, Cross Country Healthcare's Vice President of Investor Relations. Thank you, and please go ahead, sir.
Josh Vogel
VP of Investor Relations, Cross Country Healthcare
Thank you, and good afternoon, everyone. I'm joined today by our President and Chief Executive Officer, John Martins, as well as Bill Burns, our Chief Financial Officer, Dan White, Chief Commercial Officer, and Marc Krug, Group President of Delivery. Today's call will include a discussion of our financial results for Q3 2022, as well as our outlook for Q4. A copy of our earnings press release is available on our website at crosscountryhealthcare.com. Please note that certain statements made on this call may constitute forward-looking statements. These statements reflect the company's beliefs based upon information currently available to it.
As noted in our press release, forward-looking statements can vary materially from actual results and are subject to known and unknown risks, uncertainties, and other factors, including those contained in the company's 2021 annual report on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, as well as in other filings with the SEC. The company does not intend to update guidance or any of its forward-looking statements prior to the next earnings release. Additionally, we reference non-GAAP financial measures such as Adjusted EBITDA or adjusted earnings per share. Such non-GAAP financial measures are provided as additional information and should not be considered substitutes for or superior to those calculated in accordance with US GAAP. More information related to these non-GAAP financial measures is contained in our press release.
Also during this call, we may refer to pro forma when normalized numbers pertain to our most recent acquisitions as though the results were included or excluded from the periods presented. With that, I will now turn the call over to our Chief Executive Officer, John Martins.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Thanks Josh, and thank you to everyone for joining us this afternoon. Before I get started, I'd just like to take a moment to welcome the newest members of the Cross Country family that joined us this past month through our recent acquisitions of Mint and Lotus. Two physician staffing companies that we believe not only expands our market presence, but brings us a talented team of professionals to join the ranks of Cross Country Locums and sets the stage for accelerated organic growth. Welcome, Mint and Lotus. Q3 marks six months for me as CEO of Cross Country, and I am amazed and excited by what we have achieved during this time, as well as what lies ahead. As an organization, we continue to execute well across so many fronts, from sales to delivery, and across our technology initiatives.
Our unwavering commitment to always act ethically and to deliver best in class service has positioned us as an integral partner to the thousands of clients and tens of thousands of clinicians and professionals we serve. Our success is rooted in the dedication of our employees and their commitment to maintaining a vibrant workplace culture that stresses the importance of diversity, equity, and inclusion. The culture at Cross Country has never been stronger, as evidenced by our recent recognition with the Best Companies for Happiness award from Comparably. We take great pride in becoming the employer of choice for so many, and we will continue to elevate and evolve our organization by investing in our people and culture.
As noted in our press release today, we posted another strong quarter for both revenue and Adjusted EBITDA, exceeding the upper end of the guidance ranges we shared at our Investor Day event in mid-September. In addition to highlighting our outstanding leadership team, we announced full year 2023 minimum guidance and had the opportunity to share more insight into Cross Country's innovative technology and impact it is having on our business. The shift from being almost exclusively internally focused to heavier investments in externally facing technology was evidenced in the launch of Intellify, our proprietary cloud-based vendor management system, and this represents a significant milestone for the company in our evolution as a tech-enabled workforce solutions company. I'll go more into details on Intellify later in the call, but first, let me provide some comments on our Q3 results.
With consolidated revenue of $636 million, we grew by nearly 70% year-over-year, with all lines of business reporting growth. The strong revenue performance, coupled with stable gross margins and cost management, drove Adjusted EBITDA of $64 million, representing a 10% Adjusted EBITDA margin. Increasingly, our revenue growth is coming from volume as bill rates have trended down throughout the year. In fact, travel bill rates for Q3 were down 12% sequentially and down nearly 20% since Q1, though still 10% higher than a year ago. With a backdrop of continued strong demand amidst the tight labor market, travel rates have stabilized over the last several months, and we believe they are settling into a new normal for the market as anticipated.
Bill will step through the guidance a little bit later, but it's important to note that the sequential decline in travel bill rates expected for Q4 is primarily attributable to the wind down of higher rate assignments and not necessarily due to the continued decline in the bill rates. As a partner to dozens of healthcare systems, we are sensitive to their need to reduce costs for contingent labor and will continue to do all that we can to help them achieve their goals, leveraging our full complement of services, including helping them build up their core staff and offering them technology solutions such as Intellify that will help them better manage their spend. Today, our largest source of revenue comes from our managed service programs, or MSPs, representing 55% of our consolidated revenue for Q3.
Q3 spend under management from our MSPs was nearly $2 billion in annualized contingent labor spend, which is 4x the size of the programs we managed at the end of 2019. Generally, we fill all of our clients' needs through a combination of direct fill, and through a partner network of subcontractors. For Q3, Cross Country's capture rate on the $2 billion spend was 71%, which was up 200 basis points over Q2. Increasingly, our MSP clients will be able to benefit from the adoption of our proprietary vendor management system, Intellify, which enhances their visibility into their program spend. As of September, we had 10 programs live on the platform, with five more scheduled for deployment in Q4.
As we called out on Investor Day, Intellify also lowers our cost of fulfillment and will save millions of dollars annually once it is fully deployed. We currently anticipate the majority of our clients will be converted in the next 12 to 18 months, depending on our success in winning new accounts, as they would naturally be launched on Intellify as programs go live. The anticipated benefits of Intellify go well beyond cost savings, as the technology also allows us to be more competitive in the market, giving us access to capture significant incremental client spend through vendor neutral offerings, as well as technology extensions for direct license by clients for their internal use. Our tech roadmap is far from complete, but we are making terrific progress.
Year to date, we have spent more than $12 million on technology related investments, more than half of which is focused on externally facing technologies such as Intellify and our candidate portal known as Gateway. Gateway provides candidates a superior experience with real-time matching to open positions and the ability to self-select interests and schedules. Through this self-service model, we believe Gateway will also significantly improve operational productivity once fully deployed. As I'd like to say, you are never really done creating technology, but our tech transformation over the last few years is impressive. We have completely redesigned our entire ecosystem from the ground up using a data-centric model that interconnects all components within the ecosystem. Having a single tech stack enables us to provide the highest level of analytics while ensuring speed to market, as well as best in class experience for candidates, clients, and our teams.
It also provides us the foundation to build additional capabilities. On the strength of our performance, we continue to not only invest in growth through capacity and technology, as well as acquisitions such as Mint and Lotus, but we are also able to deploy capital in a more meaningful way through paying down expensive debt and repurchasing our shares of common stock. As we announced in August, our board authorized an additional $100 million repurchase program, and we quickly put that to work. Through a combination of exhausting our prior authorized plan and leveraging the new plan, we repurchased more than 1 million shares of stock before our mandatory blackout in mid-September. The average cost of shares repurchased was $24, and we have $87 million remaining under the new program.
We will continue to be opportunistic with share repurchases, balancing investments in our technology initiatives, strategic personnel, and tuck-in acquisitions that further bolster and diversify our portfolio. Looking to Q4, overall demand remains robust and well above pre-pandemic levels. It is interesting to note that despite the relatively high demand and the recent surge of pediatric respiratory cases, we are not yet seeing significant spikes in demand for seasonal needs, which could be a further tailwind as we head into the end of the year. Specific to our travel business, orders remain steady across most specialties, with growing demand for emergency room, ICU, labor and delivery, and pediatrics. Supply constraint continues to be the biggest challenge faced by our clients, with clinicians looking to retire early or leave the bedside due to fatigue and burnout.
In fact, a recent survey by Bain showed that 25% of US clinicians are considering switching careers outright, mostly due to burnout. Additionally, data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics continues to indicate a wide spread between healthcare job openings and hires. For Q4, we expect revenue to be between $590 and 600 million, well above the $550 million exit run rate we shared at our investor day. While Mint and Lotus will contribute to our performance, the majority of the increase comes from higher volumes as well as a slightly higher projected bill rates. Our Adjusted EBITDA guidance implies a margin of 9% in line with our goal to maintain Adjusted EBITDA margins in the high single to low double digits. I've called this out before, but it's worth repeating.
Though we strive for continued margin expansion every quarter, we will continue to make investments that may interrupt the trend, but we believe will ultimately drive greater shareholder value. Though we are encouraged that bill rates have stabilized, we recognize the potential for future volatility. That said, we are well positioned to continue driving organic growth thanks to the investments we have made in revenue producers, the development of market-leading technologies, and by continuing to win new clients. We therefore reiterate our targets for 2023 announced in mid-September to deliver full year 2023 revenue of at least $2.2 billion and Adjusted EBITDA in excess of $200 million. In closing, I am very encouraged by our clients, our business, and our prospects as we approach 2023.
As bill rates continue to normalize and demand remains strong, it sets up an exciting runway for long-term, sustained, profitable growth across all lines of business. I want to thank all of our dedicated professionals who made Cross Country Healthcare their employer of choice. I'd also like to thank our shareholders for believing in the company and, of course, our talented team who have supported our transformation into a high-performance tech-enabled total workforce management solutions firm. With that, let me turn the call over to Bill.
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
Thanks, John, and good afternoon, everyone. Once again, we have delivered results that have exceeded our expectations with both revenue and Adjusted EBITDA above the high end of the revised guidance issued during our investor day in mid-September. The overachievement relative to the updated guidance was driven by better than expected performance across several lines of business, including education, physician staffing, and search, as well as the impact from a small labor disruption we supported in the final weeks of the quarter. We continue to execute well across multiple fronts and experience robust year-over-year growth across all of our lines of business. As a result, consolidated revenues for the quarter was $636 million, up 70% over the prior year and down 16% sequentially.
The primary driver of our growth continues to be the number of professionals on assignment and, to a much lesser extent, the impact from rates. Gross profit was $144 million, which was up 71% over the prior year and down 16% sequentially. Gross margin of 22.6% was flat sequentially, but up 20 basis points over the prior year as we continue to see a decline in COVID-related crisis orders and a normalization in bill pay spreads across our travel business. Our solid top line performance, combined with improved productivity and operational efficiencies, fueled another quarter of strong earnings with Adjusted EBITDA of nearly $64 million, representing a margin of 10%, making it the fourth quarter in a row of delivering double-digit Adjusted EBITDA margins.
Turning to the segments, Nurse and Allied reported revenue of $612 million, representing an increase of 72% over the prior year and a 16% decline sequentially. Our largest business, Travel Nurse and Allied, was up nearly 90% over the prior year, fueled by an increase in the number of billable hours of more than 73%. The sequential decline in travel was predominantly driven by the expected decline in bill rates, which were down 12%. Looking to Q4, we anticipate average bill rates will decline once again, though at a more modest pace, likely in the high single digits. Travel demand has remained very strong, with orders continuing to be more than 10% above the start of Q3 and well ahead of pre-pandemic levels.
From a trend perspective, bill rates have leveled off and remained stable for the last four-plus months after having declined throughout most of H1. Looking into 2023, we will likely see that rates a little bit higher than we anticipated last quarter. That said, rates could step down in the future if clients see lower needs for contingent labor, though at the moment, it's hard to predict when that might happen or how it might affect our bill rates, considering the incredibly tight labor market. Our local business was up 9% from the prior year, though down 14% sequentially, with the sequential drivers fairly evenly split between rates and volume.
The majority of the volume decline has come from a drop in local contract or block book assignments returning to more normal levels for our local business following the pandemic. Also with the Nurse and Allied, our home care business rose 23% over the prior year as we continue to ramp our managed service outsourcing arrangements with several large PACE providers. Lastly, our education business reported a 38% increase over the prior year and was down 11% sequentially, due entirely to the impact from summer vacation. We remain excited at the prospects for this business to continue growing organically in the high double digits into the future. In fact, we expect the Q4 to be the single highest revenue quarter for this business in its history.
Finally, the physician staffing segment delivered nearly $24 million in revenue, which was up 27% over the prior year and 8% over the prior quarter. Billable days were up 8% over the prior year and 6% sequentially, with growth across a wide range of specialties. On a year-over-year basis, excuse me, average revenue per day filled increased across virtually all specialties as needs continue to rise. Moving down the income statement, total selling, general and administrative expense was $80 million, up 52% over the prior year and down 7% sequentially. As a percent of revenue, our SG&A was 12.6%, down nearly 150 basis points over the prior year on the improved operating leverage stemming from the growth in our business, as well as greater productivity from our revenue producers.
The majority of the increase in SG&A over the prior year was driven by continued investments in people and higher compensation on the continued strong performance of the company, as well as investments in our technology initiatives that are not capitalizable. On a sequential basis, the decline was primarily driven by lower incentive compensation associated with the sequential trend in the business, which was partly offset by continued investments in our workforce, which grew by 4% over the prior quarter. We continue to believe the market supports further investments in resources, and we will leverage our capacity planning models to ensure that they are targeted to the areas with the greatest opportunities. In addition to the investments in people, we're also investing heavily in our technology with additional resources and developers to facilitate the rapid deployment of candidate and client-facing technology like our new VMS, Intellify.
Year to date, we've spent more than $12 million on technology, and given the nature of some of the projects, roughly 60% to 70% of it qualifies for capitalization or deferral. During the quarter, we recognized $2.5 million in restructuring charges and $3.8 million in asset impairments, primarily related to the closure of additional office space during the quarter. Interest expense of $3.5 million represented a decline of 9% over Q2 on lower average borrowings across the quarter. With the majority of the remaining debt outstanding related to our subordinated term loan, our effective interest rate was 9%.
As a result of the significant cash generated during the quarter and the level of availability on our asset borrowing line, we chose to make an optional prepayment of $50 million just after the end of Q3 to reduce our interest costs further. I'll go into more detail on the capital allocation in just a moment. Finally, on the income statement, income tax expense was $14 million, representing an effective tax rate of 28.5%. Based on our latest projections, we now believe our full year effective tax rate will be between approximately 28.5% to 29%, excluding discrete items. Our profitability for the quarter resulted in adjusted earnings per share of $1.07, which was 75% higher than the prior year.
Turning to the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with $30 million in cash and $133 million in outstanding debt, including $124 million under our subordinated term loan and $9 million in borrowings under our ABL facility. Cash on hand was intentionally high as we were preparing to fund the closing of our two Locum Tenens companies, Mint and Lotus. From a cash flow perspective, we generated more than $140 million in cash from operations during the quarter, representing the single highest quarter in the company's history. Our days sales outstanding was 67 days, representing a 1-day increase over Q2, primarily due to the sequential decline in revenue relative to the timing for collections. We expect DSO will start to normalize as we progress through Q4 and into the start of 2023.
With the significant cash flows we generated, we not only reduced the overall indebtedness of the company by $76 million, but we funded the acquisitions mentioned a moment ago, repurchased more than 1 million shares of our stock at an average price of $24, as well as paid the first earn-out payment on our acquisition of WSG for having achieved the targeted results. Looking ahead, we expect to continue to generate a significant amount of cash in Q4, and as I mentioned a moment ago, have already repaid an additional $50 million of the subordinated term loan in Q4, bringing the year-to-date prepayments to $100 million. With regards to future share repurchases, we will continue to be opportunistic.
Though as we shared at our recent Investor Day, we believe the best use for cash continues to be to fund future growth. This brings me to our outlook for the Q4. We're guiding to Q4 revenue of between $590 and 600 million, representing a sequential decline of 6% to 7%, driven predominantly by the anticipated decline in travel bill rates, partly offset by growth in our education and the impact of our recent acquisitions Mint and Lotus. Gross margins are expected to be between 22.3% and 22.8%, largely consistent with the current quarter. Based on our estimated revenue and gross profit, we're expecting Adjusted EBITDA to be between $52 and 57 million, representing an Adjusted EBITDA margin of approximately 9%.
The sequential decline in Adjusted EBITDA margin is primarily due to the impact of lower average bill rates in travel, as well as continued investments in our technology initiatives and in our workforce. Adjusted earnings per share is expected to be between $0.85 and $0.95 based on an average share count of 37.1 million shares. Also assumed in this guidance is an interest expense of $3.2 million, depreciation and amortization of $3.4 million, stock-based compensation of $2.1 million, and an effective tax rate of 29%. This concludes our prepared remarks, and we would now like to open the line for questions. Operator?
Operator
Thank you. We will now begin our question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question over the phone lines, please press star one from your phone, unmute your line, and speak your name clearly when prompted. Your name and affiliation are required. If you would like to withdraw your question, press star two. Again, to ask a question over the phone lines, please press star, then one. Our first question comes from Kevin Fischbeck with Bank of America. Your line is open.
Kevin Fischbeck
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America Securities
Great, thanks. I guess maybe the first question, you know, the quarter came in better, the guidance of Q4 is coming in better, but you haven't really changed the outlook for next year. I mean, are you still thinking then that ultimately the bill rates, you know, stabilize at the same rate you thought before? Or are you now starting to think that, you know, the starting point for next year is probably gonna be higher and that there could be some upside for the next year outlook?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Sure. Hi, Kevin. Thank you for the first question of the evening. This is John. I'll start and have Bill add some more color. But yeah, when we're looking at it in terms of our guidance, or what our targets were for 2023, that was really the minimum target we were looking at that $2.2 billion and that $200 million of EBITDA. And we, at this point, again, you know, not having that perfect crystal ball in front of us, we're looking at where rates have leveled off. If we look at what happened with the rates, we saw the rates going on a decline as we went through the year.
Right now what's happening is some of the higher rates that were in the beginning of the year and through Q2, those people are coming off assignments now, and now we've leveled off those bill rates. As we see in the future, we're thinking the bill rates will remain stable at the current rate they're at. What I would say is there's a lot of different trends from the macroeconomic trends that could have impact on those rates. Of course, when we talk about rates, I'd be remiss not to talk about the supply and demand that really causes the rates to fluctuate. Because there's such a wide spread between the demand and supply and balance, there's a lot of volatility that could happen in next year.
As of now, this $2.2 billion of revenue is the floor we see, and we do think that there is potential upside to this, but we're also cautious to say that there could be some headwinds of macroeconomic trends that could impact that. When you look at this $2.2 billion dollar minimum floor we have, you know, could you even think of that, of us hitting that ball right down the center of the fairway. Bill, would you like to add some comments?
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah, sure. Hey, thanks, Kevin. John made the point I was gonna make, which is it was minimum guidance as we called out. Look, there's a lot of unknowns as we look at 2023. You know, the potential for further economic disruption, the potential pullback in some demand for contingent labor, although again, not seeing that today. Is it possible rates could go down a little bit further? Of course. I mean, if you recall earlier this year, we had thought it would be a sequential double-digit decline. We're now calling for a high single. There's a little bit more room we would anticipate that is there potentially on the rate side. After four months of kind of seeing the stability in the rates, it's hard to see when that might play out that way.
To John's point, there is some potential upside there. I remind you know, the other lines of business are growing well. We're seeing phenomenal growth in our home care, out of our education, our search businesses. That's why we've not changed the $2.2 billion. I think as we get through the Q4, we'll obviously look to give you a little bit better lens on 2023.
Kevin Fischbeck
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America Securities
Okay, that's helpful. I guess you mentioned that some of the variability in bill rates is due to changes in the crisis orders as a percentage of total. Is there a way to kinda give us that number? Where was that as a percentage of total orders in Q3, and what was that normally like in 2019 and pre-pandemic?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
You know, Kevin, we've stopped actually tracking things as crisis orders. I'd say that in Q3, even if I look at the labor disruption rates that we saw, they were not, like, remarkably different than what we're seeing in the broader marketplace. The market is settling into a more of a premium rate relative to pre-pandemic. I wouldn't call them necessarily premium rates today. It's really just what the market is demanding. You know, as far as splitting it down, it'd be an arbitrary split to tell you how the percentages are shaking out relative to pre-pandemic, because we simply are not flagging orders as premium rate orders or crisis orders.
Kevin Fischbeck
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America Securities
Maybe just last question. You mentioned that the pediatric respiratory cases aren't coming in the seasonally the way that you... I mean, we hear a lot about it, I guess, in the news about the triple whatever they're calling it now. Is that because... Are the hospitals just waiting to actually kinda see it fully come through before they ask for that staff? Is there a reason why they wouldn't be staffing up in front of that? Any color there?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Sure. I'll start, and then maybe Marc, you wanna add.
Marc Krug
Group President of Delivery, Cross Country Healthcare
Sure.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
But as we said, we're seeing cases come up, and obviously you watch the news in the media, right? What you're seeing is tons of patients being diverted and going 70 miles to get to a hospital. We are seeing an uptick in pediatric specialties, but not at the surge that we would've expected with the triple threat of RSV, of the flu and a little bit of COVID in there.
What you know what we're anticipating that could happen to be a scenario, these children are getting this through this triple threat, and now as we're heading towards the holidays, you have Thanksgiving and the December holidays coming up, plus in most of the country, it's going to become a little colder and more people will be inside. We think that triple threat has the potential to really cause an increase in demand towards the end of the year and year. Now, when we look at our numbers of $2.2 billion for next year, these potential tailwinds are not baked into those numbers at all.
Of course, we're hoping that this doesn't come to fruition, but we are very well prepared with the capacity of our recruitment team, with our sales folks going out to potential new clients to make sure that we can help serve the communities, the hospitals, and the patients at the bedside if it comes to fruition that we have this triple threat surge move into the adult population as well. Marc or Dan, do you wanna add anything to that?
Marc Krug
Group President of Delivery, Cross Country Healthcare
Sure, John. I mean, we have seen most recently a sharp increase in the pediatric respiratory orders. Probably not as strong or as high as we would've expected at this point, but overall pediatric order volume has increased almost 20% since the start of Q4. That's more in line with what we expect.
Dan White
Chief Commercial Officer, Cross Country Healthcare
This is Dan. What I will add is that we have a decent number of children's facilities that are in our pipeline for sales, and one of the things that we like to do is to have capacity to help those customers that are in our pipeline. We're getting reached out to kind of in a real-time basis right now for assistance on some of those specialties specifically.
Kevin Fischbeck
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America Securities
All right, great. Thank you.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
You bet.
Kevin Fischbeck
Managing Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America Securities
Okay.
Operator
Our next question comes from A.J. Rice with Credit Suisse. Your line is open.
A.J. Rice
Managing Director of Equity Research, Credit Suisse
Thanks. Hi, everybody. Maybe just trying to get my arms around the market dynamics again. You know, I think you guys may have been the ones that had said earlier in the year that, maybe in the early part of the summer, the rates had gotten to a level where some travel nurses were saying, "Hey, at that level, I'm just gonna go back into my permanent job." Or, how much of a constraint is that on seeing declining rates, the fact that it hasn't declined? Are we at a point now where if it were to continue to decline, it would start to drive some nurses back?
Another dynamic we sometimes see, or we saw many years ago at this point, is nurses get nervous about whether their permanent job is still available to them and begin to think that maybe they should go back. I wondered if the economic backdrop is unsettled enough or not really, that may be part of the equation in what you're seeing on nurses that are out on travel but wondering whether they should go back. Is that entered into the equation at all?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Sure. Hey, A.J., it's John. I would say that when we look at where we are with the core nurses that moved out of their core positions to move into travel, sure, some of them definitely went back, you know, after Q2 and into Q3, went back to their core jobs. We don't believe that these nurses are thinking it's like musical chairs, that if they don't go back into their job, into a core job, there won't be any chairs left. When we look at the macroeconomic trends, you know, unemployment is still at a historic low. When we look at the JOLTS BLS data, if we look at from the Affordable Care Act in 2014 to today, open positions have increased by 233%.
When we look at the ratio of open jobs to hires from the BLS JOLTS data, historically, that number has been a ratio of less than two and probably somewhere between 1.5 to 1.7. It hit a high in March of about 2.94, and currently in September, it stands at about 2.8. The clinicians that we're speaking to, they realize there's a lot of jobs out there. Hospitals, of course, understand that they need to hire for the core staff. At Cross Country, what we're really doing is we're looking at how we can help hospitals really solve the challenges of the core staff.
Because if you look at the studies that have been out there, I think it was McKinsey, I believe, who had a study a couple of months ago that said there's a 400,000 nurse shortage today in the United States. Then if we look at, you know, every study, and we talk about this all the time, right? If we look at all the different studies out there over the last, you know, year or two, in the next 10 years, there's gonna be a 1 million nurse shortage. The demand is there, the demand will continue to be there. For us, it's working with hospitals to say, how can we upskill clinicians to get into acute care? How can we create more preceptors and educators to create more supply into the hospitals?
What we're looking at is for the foreseeable future, there is going to be this incredible chasm of supply-demand imbalance that's just not going to go away. Even if we were to have a macroeconomic downturn, it would take a lot for it to turn from this historic high demand, where unemployment rates would have to be pretty significantly high, for clinicians to say, "Hey, I'm gonna return to a permanent job." Dan?
Dan White
Chief Commercial Officer, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah. I, A.J., this is Dan. I would like to sort of add to what John said. I think everybody realizes that we have an RPO and search division, which does in fact help people, our customers with filling their permanent positions. You know, that business itself is, you know, somewhere between $25 to 30 million now, up over 60% year over year. We have a huge opportunity to help our customers with these problems. It's beneficial to us to do that. I would say about 80% of that is our RPO business, which is more consistent in a recurring revenue. For us, it's kinda a little bit of both sides of the equation.
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
A.J., this is Bill. If I could just put a point on that, we're seeing it in relation to our numbers and that we don't guide at the business level. For us, sequentially in Q4, we're expecting volumes to essentially be flat. So we're not seeing a falloff in HCPs or healthcare professionals, you know, willing to take assignments. So that's how we see the Q4 shaping out.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah. A.J., just to add to all of that, we did see renewal rates drop in Q2, which means a portion were going back to their core jobs. At this point, we are seeing them back up, which, you know, for me, means it's probably leveled off at this point as rates have stabilized.
A.J. Rice
Managing Director of Equity Research, Credit Suisse
Okay. Maybe just looking at the other side of the coin, we're reading so much about hospitals facing downgrades, swinging to operating losses. You said that, you know, hospitals are hurting out there, but they obviously need nurses to service the patients, or it's just a vicious spiral. Any interesting aspects to that discussion, ways they're leaning on you that may be different than history to try to figure out ways to address the current environment in which they find themselves?
Dan White
Chief Commercial Officer, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah. A.J., this is Dan. I'll maybe start that and see if anyone else wants to add in some color. Just this past quarter, we started a team that does workforce optimization for our clients. We'll go in, do an assessment of kinda how their utilization is working on a unit-by-unit basis across the system, and then give them advice for how exactly, you know, to fill those gaps, if you will. We're building technology that helps us take that currently very manual process and make it a deeper part of our Intellify platform. Ultimately, what we wanna have for our customers is, you know, manage your core staff better, supplement that with regional or local float pool resources, and then bring on your travelers to augment that.
So far, the reception on that process, if you will, is really high, both from existing customers and prospective customers.
A.J. Rice
Managing Director of Equity Research, Credit Suisse
Okay, great. Thanks so much.
Dan White
Chief Commercial Officer, Cross Country Healthcare
You bet.
Operator
Our next question comes from Brian Tanquilut with Jefferies. Your line is open.
Brian Tanquilut
Senior Equity Analyst, Jefferies
Hey, good morning, guys. Oh, good afternoon, guys, and congrats on the quarter. I guess just a question again on the bill rates. Is there a seasonality factor that we should be thinking about? I mean, I appreciate that it's been flattish for the past few weeks, but any thoughts on seasonality and pricing that we should consider?
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
Hey, Brian, it's Bill. Thanks. No, I don't think there's a real seasonality to our bill rates, certainly not across the travel business. We don't typically see that at any point in our history. I know that in the last couple of years, it's hard to point to history and say that that's a good predictor. We do not normally see a seasonal fluctuation in bill rates. There may be on specialty needs, and there may be geographic needs that vary throughout the year, but not on the bill rates.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah, I would just add to that, Brian. This is John. I think what Bill said is, you know, the geographical and the regional rates have changed. I think when we looked at COVID.
During most of that two-year period with a national rate because everyone had the same surge in demand. Now, even with pediatrics, we're seeing pockets of areas that get hit with the triple threat. Now it's spreading more and more, so it may become a national price, but I think regionalization pricing is really what we're seeing more of.
Brian Tanquilut
Senior Equity Analyst, Jefferies
Got it. Okay. The last thing about the locums business, I mean, any feedback so far that you've heard from your clients in terms of cross-sell opportunities as you try to get bigger and deeper in that locum space?
Dan White
Chief Commercial Officer, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah, I'll take that one, Brian. This is Dan. We absolutely are getting tons of interest from customers for physicians. Obviously, that helps them on the revenue side of their equation and so on and so forth. The other thing that I would say is that from a cross-selling opportunity, we don't have locums in most of our MSPs. In fact, it's one of the best areas and one of the reasons why, you know, we wanted to add this capability. What I might add, too, is just from an integration perspective, we're already seeing those teams fill each other's orders, if you follow me. You know, the existing locums team here at Cross Country is filling orders that were with both Lotus and Mint and vice versa.
The kind of integration leverage we're getting out of this is incredibly high, which, again, gives us, you know, more confidence to go into our customer base.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah, this is John. I would just add that also with the acquisitions of Mint and Lotus, that's really helped us create more capacity than we've had before. That business, if we look at where that business is trending, Brian, it's gonna be, you know, roughly $150 million business, giving us more capacity to help us be able to bring that offering to our clients in a larger scale than we could have ever done before.
Brian Tanquilut
Senior Equity Analyst, Jefferies
Awesome. Thanks, guys.
Dan White
Chief Commercial Officer, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah.
Operator
Our next question comes from Tobey Sommer with Truist Securities. Your line is open.
Tobey Sommer
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Thank you. Wanted to start on gross margins. When do you expect gross margin compression to end, and what kind of strategies do you have in mind to sort of claw some of that gross margin back?
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
Hey, Tobey. This is Bill. Well, look, I think, you know, part of it is it's always a competitive dynamic. You're in competition for the healthcare professional, so we're always gonna have to make sure that we have a market pay rate that moves along with it. We can see that the pay rates have come down slightly faster than the bill rates. The stubborn piece has been the housing cost, and as you can imagine, with the inflation backdrop, you know, that's the piece that is gonna be a little bit harder to, you know, claw back, as you call it. I think the opportunities really lie around other efficiencies within our gross profit. If you think about Intellify, for example, that's set to save us millions of dollars.
In the last part of the Q3 and going into the Q4, we've already begun the conversion of a number of accounts, and they've gotten north of $100 million in spend actually migrated onto the platform. That's gonna drive annual savings just from what we've already migrated of over $1 million annually. Obviously, we've got a roadmap to do that throughout the Q4 and into the H1 of 2023. And then, of course, there's other efficiencies. You know, we look at everything up and down the line across, whether it's our professional liability insurances, our workers' comp insurances, the credentialing costs that we have. A lot of it's gonna be looking across those opportunities.
Of course, you know, the broader consolidated impact will come from improving, continuing to improve the mix. Any other comments, John?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah. Hey, Tobey. This is John. Yeah, I would just say, as Bill said, we're going to keep increasing our diversification. If we look at our WSG or Workforce Solutions Group that works in the pay centers and home health, that's a business that is also going to be north of $100 million, and that's a higher margin business as we continue to invest in those other peripheral businesses of ours, that grow as we're getting them to grow at a faster rate, that'll help drive gross margins.
I think really what's going to propel us to drive gross margins even faster is our movement and entry into the vendor neutral space with Intellify. Now, we announced that on our Investor Day that we're moving into this vendor neutral space. It's, you know, somewhere between a $10 to 20 billion market where we have zero penetration in. As we build, we're building a pretty long, big pipeline right now in MSPs and our vendor neutral business, Intellify, that's going to help us increase our gross margins and our EBITDA margins because those vendor neutral businesses are very highly profitable in the GM, gross margin side, as well as the EBITDA side.
Tobey Sommer
Managing Director, Truist Securities
That's helpful from a mix standpoint. If I think about the travel and allied business as it's currently formulated, how do your gross margins, you know, either in the quarter or implied in your guidance compare to what you think, you know, 2023 looks like in that business? Just trying to get a sense for whether there is a rebound in the offing or you know, is there further compression that you expect?
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
I don't think there's further compression, Tobey. I think, you know, it today, and remember, intentionally, we've opted to give the majority of the compensation through to the nurse. So our margins have been depressed a little bit in that business. We've seen it in the low twenties kind of range for our gross margin across travel. I think that while we're still down a couple of hundred basis points, I don't anticipate getting all that back in 2023. I do think that there's room for, let's call it somewhere in that, you know, 100 basis point improvement over the next, you know, 12 months. But Marc, anything you-
Marc Krug
Group President of Delivery, Cross Country Healthcare
No, you know, I think it's gonna be slow and gradual. I don't expect it to be overnight, but I think, you know, I don't expect any further compression. To John's point earlier, our other businesses, the education division, is a high margin business, and it's actually a great story. It's up almost 70% Q3 2022 versus Q3 2019. Q4 shaping up to be our best quarter ever. We're seeing diversification there as well. Paraprofessionals are our fastest-growing segment within the education business. Demand has shifted a little bit. Traditionally we saw strong demand for speech-language pathologists and special ed professionals, but we're also seeing today very strong demand in mainstream teachers and paraprofessionals where we enjoy great margins.
Tobey Sommer
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Thank you. How did the volume of travelers in Q3, which looks like it's down about 7% quarter-over-quarter, compared to your expectations when you gave guidance for the Q3?
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah, it's a good question, Tobey. I'd say it was probably a little bit deeper decline than we had anticipated. If I go back to when we first gave our guidance, it was down just a little bit more significantly, but as we look across where that came from, it was the wind down of higher bill rate assignments. You know, we've seen good production across the weeks, you know, throughout the tail end of Q3 as we're going into Q4. I think it was really just a step down from the crisis needs from the COVID pandemic.
Tobey Sommer
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Yeah.
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
I don't think it was anything more significant than that.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah. I'd add probably from towards the end of Q2 to the middle of Q3 is probably where we saw a little bit of dip in our volume production, which we didn't anticipate as deep of a volume production. Then we had the steady increase in demand, and now our production is catching up to that.
Tobey Sommer
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Perfect. Last one from me. Could you comment, John, about what you're thinking about in terms of the timing of deploying some of this cash? You did buy some stock and then put it on halt. The stock kind of went on a tear right after you bought some. So that's understandable. Are multiples coming down from private companies sufficiently such that you could continue to do acquisitions that are accretive like the bolt-ons you did in position?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Without a doubt, yes. Also on the buyback program, yes, our stock did have a run, but we also were in our mandatory blackout period, so that's the reason why we halted buying. Yes, we did have a nice run on the stock. Yeah. Look, when we look at where we're gonna be in 2023 and beyond, acquisitions are a large part of what we'll be doing with our capital deployment. You know, we're slowly seeing multiples coming down. I anticipate we'll see multiples continue to come down, especially, you know, if the broader economic conditions fall unfavorable. Yeah, we're still very active in the M&A market.
Tobey Sommer
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Thank you.
Operator
Our final question comes from Kevin Steinke with Barrington Research. Your line is open.
Kevin Steinke
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, Barrington Research
Good afternoon. I just wanted to ask about your plans for recruiter hiring over the next several quarters, the volume you think you have to add there and any challenges in finding staff, any upward pressure on compensation costs, et cetera.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Hey, Kevin, this is John. I will start and hand it over to Marc Krug. To start, we're always looking at our capacity model that we have that kind of shows recruiter productivity or producer productivity with how much demand there is. It's kind of a formula that we have, an algorithm that shows what we need. Look, we're a growth company, and we'll continue to invest in people, and we're gonna continue to invest where demand is. As long as demand stays as strong and continues to increase, we're going to be hiring producers, not only in our Nurse and Allied business, but in education, in locums, in our WSG business, in our RPO and search business. You know, we will continue to invest in those. Marc, did you have any?
Marc Krug
Group President of Delivery, Cross Country Healthcare
Sure. Hey, Kevin. You know, at this point, we really don't have challenges finding staff because we're virtual now, so it's a much bigger pool to select from. We're finding great talent. You know, our compensation costs are steady. They haven't changed a whole lot. Recruiter productivity is still very strong, almost double what it was pre-pandemic. As long as that's the case, you know, we're gonna continue to top grade higher, and make sure we have enough capacity.
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
Kevin, this is Bill. Just two quick points. One, I did mention the prepared remarks that we did grow our staff 4% in Q3. So that's just, you know, one quarter of sequential change. That was quite an investment we made. Of course, most of those were in revenue producers.
Just to dovetail into Marc's comment, you know, when you look at our comp structure, I think we're among the most competitive in the marketplace. We give our folks the ability to earn more as they grow their books of business. I think it's, that's part of what helps it be very attractive for folks to join Cross Country.
Kevin Steinke
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, Barrington Research
All right. Yeah, that's helpful. You mentioned their recruiter productivity, and I believe you've mentioned that as a contributing factor to the margin improvement in the quarter. Just wondering how much more room there is to run in terms of improving recruiter productivity. I know newer people can ramp up faster, but just as you look at the staff overall, is there more room to run there on productivity improvement?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
This is John again. I'll start and hand off to Bill and Marc. I think, you know, with our continuing investment in technology, especially with our Gateway portal, which we had, you know, rolled out in April this year rather, and we talked a lot more about it on Investor Day. There's a lot of room and runway for us to have more productivity. As we start really becoming a more self-service model for clinicians, our producers will be able to have larger capacity gains, which will flow right through the bottom line to our EBITDA, lowering SG&A, and increasing higher EBITDA. I know Bill and Marc wanna comment.
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
I was just gonna say the same thing, John. I think when you look at the initial driver of the big gains we've had in productivity, you would tie it back to the applicant tracking system we put in for travel. That's just one piece of the puzzle, and there's obviously other levers that we're looking to pull.
Marc Krug
Group President of Delivery, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah. In addition to what they said, what John and Bill said, we're also doing enhancements to the applicant tracking system right now, and that's really helping drive productivity. We're tweaking the organization to fuel growth and making sure revenue producers focus on revenue-producing activity.
Kevin Steinke
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, Barrington Research
All right. Thanks for taking the questions. Appreciate it.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Thank you.
Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, this does conclude the Q&A period. I'll now turn it back over to John Martins for closing remarks.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Thank you. In closing, I'd like to thank everyone for participating in today's call. We look forward to updating you on our progress on the next call in February. See you then.
Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, this does conclude today's conference. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.

Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Cross Country Healthcare's Earnings Conference Call for Q1 2022. I would now like to turn the call over to Josh Vogel, Cross Country Healthcare's Vice President, Investor Relations. Thank you, and please go ahead, sir.
Josh Vogel
VP of Investor Relations, Cross Country Healthcare
Thank you and good afternoon, everyone. I'm joined today by our President and Chief Executive Officer, John Martins, as well as Bill Burns, our Chief Financial Officer, Dan White, Chief Commercial Officer, Buffy White, Group President of Workforce Solutions, and Marc Krug, Group President of Delivery.
Today's call will include a discussion of our financial results for Q1 2022 as well as our outlook for Q2. A copy of our earnings press release is available on our website at crosscountryhealthcare.com. Please note that certain statements made on this call may constitute forward-looking statements. President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Well, I think what we're saying is we're actually gonna see volume growth quarter-over-quarter into Q2.
A.J. Rice
Managing Director, Credit Suisse
Right.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Right.
A.J. Rice
Managing Director, Credit Suisse
Yeah.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
A.J., I think if your question is, you know, about the rates, so you're right. I think that the rates we called out, what we're seeing expecting for Q2 in that kinda mid-single digit, high single digit, I'll call it, range. As the rates are coming down, it does take time, especially in travel with longer term assignments, right? These are 13-week assignments.
The impact is not as significant in Q2, but we're still projecting them to come down. I'd say if you were to seasonalize this throughout the year, probably Q3 is where we'll see this, the larger sequential drop and then a smaller drop in Q4. All within the range we called out, that low single to double, low double-digit kinda sequential declines into the balance of the year.
It's just, it's really about the sequencing and the timing of when the rates come down. You know, it's a function of whether the assignments that have the higher bill rates are canceling and/or being replaced at new bill rates. The bill rate on open orders is down. We have seen that already begin, but the rate at which it's bleeding into the revenue stream because of how it trends off, it takes a little bit more time for that to be seen.
A.J. Rice
Managing Director, Credit Suisse
Okay. To the extent that you're a little more positive on the placements, going into the Q2, is that being driven by patient volumes or nurses at the facility level stepping back or what?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
No, you know, look, it is demand that is. When we look at it, as we just, you know, mentioned, it's truly the deferred healthcare. It's surgeries coming back online. It is, you know, the fundamental shortages of clinicians. You know, there was a study at the end of last year where 83% of healthcare executives said they expect long-term shortages for clinicians. It's really the fundamental shortages is what's driving this demand and driving our placements.
Operator
Our next question.
A.J. Rice
Managing Director, Credit Suisse
Okay. I also had to ask, maybe can you give us a little bit of an update on where fill rates are versus what you saw exiting the year versus now?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Sorry, A.J., could you repeat that question there?
A.J. Rice
Managing Director, Credit Suisse
Yeah, sorry. Any update on where you're at with respect to fill rates, as you exited Q1 compared to where you were in Q4, perhaps, or some other metrics. Are you filling a greater percentage of your open orders, or is it about the same as what you saw in Q4?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
You know, I would say there are so many orders in Q4. When you look at fill rates, it's really not about fill rates as it is about filling the orders we need to fill to have growth. We look at fill rates when we look at our MSPs and our exclusive orders that we need to fill because we have an obligation to our clients. In Travel Nurse and Allied, because of the number of orders we have in Travel Nurse and Allied, it's hard to look at the overall fill rate because there's just too many orders. We can have high sequential growth and exponential growth on less orders than you would think we would need.
We don't need, you know, 40,000, 50,000 orders to grow exponentially.
Marc Krug
Group President of Delivery, Cross Country Healthcare
A.J., I think I'd just give one more piece of data that might help you understand the sequential growth. We grew sequentially throughout the quarter. Our travelers on assignment continued to grow each and every month of the quarter. We exit the quarter higher than we came into Q1. That helps give the uplift into Q2. We're coming in stronger just because of the level of production that we had through Q1.
A.J. Rice
Managing Director, Credit Suisse
Okay. Just a final question. Any updated thoughts on capital deployment, deal pipeline, areas you might be interested in pursuing M&A?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah. Yeah. You know what? We're sticking very closely to our strategic plans on M&A. You know, we've said before, and we're looking at, again, locums-type companies, allied-type companies, local staffing-type companies, technology-type companies. We really take a very disciplined approach to M&A, making sure that it's a strategic fit and that it'll be accretive to our business. You know, there's plenty of opportunities out there, and we'll be looking at those opportunities to really reinforce Cross Country and our offerings.
A.J. Rice
Managing Director, Credit Suisse
Okay, great. Thanks a lot.
Operator
Our next question comes from Tobey Sommer from Truist Securities. Tobey, your line is open.
Jasper Bibb
Equity Research Associate, Truist Securities
Hey, good afternoon. This is Jasper Bibb for Toby. I want to follow up on MSP fill rates. As the market starts to level off from an order perspective, are you seeing recruiters able to capture more of that wallet share internally?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah. Hey, Jasper, this is John. We can, but it's incremental. Really what we do is what the beauty about the MSP is we can go up or down to have higher capture rate as we need. Right now, what we do is with our partner network that we use, our supplier network, we actually have them fill part of the needs.
What we do with our excess capacity is we're able to utilize that to bring in new clients and new MSPs. At a certain point, yes, if we needed to, we could ratchet up our fill rate or our capture rate. At this point, we want to keep it at that 70% that we're at so that the excess capacity we could utilize to bring in more clients.
Jasper Bibb
Equity Research Associate, Truist Securities
Thanks. I was just hoping you could speak to how you're managing customer relationships as the hospitals are saying, you know, reducing the usage of contract labor from a mix perspective is gonna be a priority for them in H2.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Sure. Well, I think it would be a great opportunity to have Dan White, our new Chief Commercial Officer, give a little color on that.
Dan White
Chief Commercial Officer, Cross Country Healthcare
Well, thanks, John. I really appreciate it. Josh, thanks for the question. You know, as we've talked about in our prepared remarks, we've had, you know, a beautiful transformation of our delivery capability, which shows in all of these terrific results that we're achieving.
Anybody who knows me very well realizes that my word is really everything to me, so that when I give my word to a client or a prospect about how we're gonna perform, I have 100% confidence that we have best-in-class delivery, and that's truly table stakes for us now. When I think about, you know, my expertise here, it really starts with transforming our client-facing teams and a focus on customer obsession.
One of the reasons I chose to join John and the team here is because of the way we serve our customers and our clinicians and sort of how we help them through all of these very difficult times. You know, I've known John for a long time. I'm getting to know these team members here really well, and all of us share a focus on the customer in the very same way.
You know, for example, partially answering your question, some of the things we heard at the Becker's conference last week were, you know, customers are looking for partners that are digital first, transparent, analytics- and performance-driven, focused on culture, and other aspects that are gonna help them with their whole workforce challenge. For me, that company today is Cross Country.
You know, when I think about our client needs and the diversity of solutions that we have, I believe that we're ready to help them solve those problems.
Jasper Bibb
Equity Research Associate, Truist Securities
No, that's great. Last question for me is, I was hoping you could provide a bit more color on cash flow dynamics as revenue starts to come off that Q1 peak.
I mean, by my math, receivables are more than 70% of your enterprise value, which should give you some options from a capital deployment perspective.
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah, Jasper, it's a good point. I mean, look, as you know, our working capital model is. We're a payroll-driven company, so it really all is on the receivable side. As revenue starts to level off and to start to see sequential declines, we do anticipate seeing some significant cash flow generation with cash from operations. Q2, you know, being the hardest one to predict right now, simply because we go into the quarter with revenue down somewhat, but we also start making some pretty large estimated tax payments for the first time. I called out in my prepared remarks, we have a $40 million estimated tax payment.
That'll be Q1 we've ever had a cash tax payment of that magnitude, given the success of the company over the last two years. We've burned through our NOLs. That's gonna hit us in Q2. As we move through H2, as we also said in the prepared remarks, we do expect very positive cash flows to be coming off as the receivables start to wind their way down. That'll be largely off of the rate decline that we're talking about because, you know, we do anticipate the volume will still be there, but if rates don't decline as we anticipate, then the cash flow generation may not be as significant as what we call out.
The opportunity is if you just did simple math and said, okay, you know, a 60-day DSO, you had $789 million of revenue in Q1, and we're saying something north of 500, you know, you can pick your number. That delta from those two numbers, and you kinda do the math, and you say, "Okay, what's, you know, roughly, 2/3 of that gonna come in as cash flow?" It's a substantial amount of cash to be collected. I will say that, you know, I don't have any concerns around our portfolio. We're very active with our clients. We're working very closely with them. From that perspective, you know, it all seems like it's going to come in, you know, as expected.
Jasper Bibb
Equity Research Associate, Truist Securities
Thanks for taking the questions, guys. I'll take the rest offline.
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
All right.

Just as a reminder, if you would like to ask a question, please dial star one, unmute your phone, and record your name clearly. Our last question in queue comes from Bill Sutherland from The Benchmark Company. Bill, your line is open.
Bill Sutherland
Director of Research, Benchmark
Thank you. Hey, everybody. Maybe give the mic back to Dan for a second because I'd just like to hear a little bit about kind of the size of your MSP operation at this point and kinda what the marketplace looks like as far as gaining new deals. Dan White
Chief Commercial Officer, Cross Country Healthcare
Well, first of all, I appreciate the question and nice to hear your voice again, Bill.
Bill Sutherland
Director of Research, Benchmark
Mm-hmm.
Dan White
Chief Commercial Officer, Cross Country Healthcare
I think in general, I'll go back to the opening remarks around, you know, the business run rate right now is a little north of $2 billion in terms of our spend under management run rate. What's nice about that is that the number of customers we have that don't have some of the services that we already deliver is a fairly significant percentage.
We can sell into the base that we already have that know and love and trust our brand and grow simply from there. On top of that, I would say there's at least 20% to 25% of the market that doesn't use any sort of MSP or VMS today, maybe more. There are certainly areas of opportunity for us to grow and help customers learn that they need to use programs like this.
I think the pandemic really helped them understand that efficiencies of technology, process improvement, you know, augmenting their internal teams with expertise outside their organization really can help speed and value to the health system. You know, of course, there's opportunity always to, you know, gain share and grow from other people's, you know, share. But I don't think that's necessary here for us to achieve the kinda numbers that we're really trying to achieve, which really makes us a growth company. At the end of the day, you know, that's why I'm here.
Bill Sutherland
Director of Research, Benchmark
Understood. Thanks for that. So what's the rough size of the education business right now, and kinda where are you focusing the growth in that sector?
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
Sorry, was that a question to myself? This is Bill. I'll answer it. I mean, look, you know, the business is, because of the summer break, it's hard to give you. I can't just take the Q1 and annualize. You have to recognize that there's a couple of months in there where they don't have the revenue. You know, they're doing probably between $15 million and $20 million during the quarters when schools are in session, probably a little bit north, towards the north end of that, so rapidly growing. I'd say the growth in that area has really been predominantly in charter schools, although increasingly servicing public school districts and increasingly serving schools outside of the state of California as well.
California was the first market we really were in, and again, it goes back to the acquisition we did in 2015, but we've steadily expanded the school base outside of that state. We offer a full range of services, everything from the clinical side to helping with the non-clinical, special education, and the like, so.
Bill Sutherland
Director of Research, Benchmark
Mm-hmm.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Bill, this is John Martins. What I'd add to that is we're seeing tremendous demand in this education business, and we're making heavy investments in there. Because when we look at what's happening in education, it runs a very similar parallel to what happened in healthcare over the last two years with the nursing shortage and the clinician shortage. These educators have been fatigued and burned out and are seeing a high level of quits. The reason why is they had online learning, then they had to go into schools, had to have PPE. A lot of teachers decided to leave the field. Right now, there is a crisis of shortages of teachers.
Which is for, they're saying, which will be around for the next, you know, several years. We think it's an opportunity for us to really help schools ramp up with their staffing, and we're making heavy investments to capture that market.
Bill Burns
EVP and CFO, Cross Country Healthcare
It was one of the reasons behind the acquisition we completed in December for the cloud-based, you know, search tool that allows educators and clinicians to find the jobs and for schools to, you know, be able to access a large candidate database for direct hire.
Bill Sutherland
Director of Research, Benchmark
You're really gonna kind of push on the educator placements as well as the healthcare going forward.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yes. I'm sorry to cut you off. As we diversify our business, yes. Education and healthcare are the two main places that we'll be investing in.
Bill Sutherland
Director of Research, Benchmark
Just one last one, just get back to the core business. As the demand for contractors inevitably eases, do you think one offset will be increasing fill rate? Because right now, you know, the demand is so far in excess of supply, right? Will that be part of the equalizer for you guys?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Yeah. It will definitely be part of the equalizer to increase fill rate. You know what also I think is going to help us really is we're investing. We talked a lot about how we invested internally about producer productivity. What we haven't spoken about a lot is how we're investing externally in technologies to help our clinicians and our clients.
A matter of fact, we just launched in January our self-service job portal for clinicians. What this self-service portal does is it helps professionals are able to view transparent pay packages. They're able to submit interest in specific assignments. They're able to self onboard to a submission rate. They're able to view their pay rates. They're able to update their credentials.
We see that there's a lot of promise that we'll be able to add the supply, bring in, making it easier for us to have fill rates and have higher fill rates. The success we've seen from this self-service portal in this soft launch that we had in the, you know, from Q1 to today, we have several thousand daily active users who are logging in each day, and those daily users are looking at over 50,000 and having 50,000 job searches per week. Those daily users are having job interest submits of over 1,000 per day. When we look at how we're going to increase the fill rate, it'll be doing so through a self-service technology.
We are just in the early innings of this technology, and we're so excited to be able to, you know, to continue to invest in this technology, which will really change fundamentally how Cross Country does business.
Bill Sutherland
Director of Research, Benchmark
Do the other major firms have this self-service kind of portal?
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
You know what? Some do and some don't. I'll tell you what, how we're investing and what we're doing. Whatever's out there, we'll be leapfrogging them, you know, in the next couple of quarters. I'm sure for sure.
Bill Sutherland
Director of Research, Benchmark
Okay. Thanks a lot for the comments. Nice job on the quarter.
John Martins
President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Thank you, Bill.

Ladies and gentlemen, this does conclude the Q&A period. I will now turn it back over to John Martins for closing remarks.

President and CEO, Cross Country Healthcare
Thank you, Madison. It's clear that we are a very different company from three years ago, and it's clear that we are a very different company than from just 18 months ago. Lastly, I wanna recognize and celebrate National Nurses Month, and I personally wanna thank every nurse out there for your hard work and dedication. Thank you everyone, and I look forward to our next earnings call.

Ladies and gentlemen, this does conclude today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
